What Is a Distribution Diagnostic? One Week, Explained

Guidelowob research

By lowob · 4 May 2026 · 7-minute read · Distribution

In short: A distribution diagnostic is a short, paid, scoped piece of work that answers which channels can carry a product to its buyer, what each costs, and where the next serious money should go. It has a fixed duration, price and written output, runs small real tests, and carries no obligation to continue. It differs from the free alternatives because someone pays for it: the European agency association found an average new-business pitch costs an agency about €43,800, and that cost is recovered in the engagement that follows. A week can show whether a channel is open and converts at all. It cannot replace the four to six weeks Google recommends for a controlled experiment.

Key points

  • A diagnostic answers one written question: which channels can carry this product, at what cost, and where the next serious money should go.
  • It includes a band map of channels, a read of what exists, two or three small parallel tests, and a written answer with the next step priced.
  • Channel access is set platform by platform and country by country, and it changes: Google opened crypto exchange ads in Argentina in 2025 and Indonesia in 2026, each with certification and local licensing.
  • One week cannot show long-run customer value, seasonality, behaviour at ten times the volume, or whether a restricted approval will arrive.
  • Insist on a fixed price and end date, tracking in your own name, and the next step priced in the same document.

Companies are offered "audits," "assessments," "discovery," and "free strategy sessions" constantly. Most are sales conversations with a document attached. A diagnostic is a different thing, and the difference is worth understanding before paying for one, or accepting a free one.

The definition

A distribution diagnostic is a short, paid, scoped piece of work that answers a specific question: which channels can carry this product to its buyer, what does each one cost, and where should the next serious money go. It has a fixed duration, a fixed price, a written output, and no obligation to continue.

We sell one as the Sounding, a one-week paid distribution diagnostic. The mechanics below are the ones we use, and they are the ones a company can use to evaluate anyone else's.

What it includes

A band map. For each channel and geography that matters, whether the platform carries the category openly, with conditions, or not at all, and what any conditions require. Written down, so it can be argued with.

A read of what exists. The current tracking, the accounts, the data, the content, the partner relationships, and the claims the company can substantiate. Not an audit of everything, but enough to know what a channel test can be built on.

Two or three small tests, run in parallel. Each in an open-band channel, each with a written question and a threshold, each with tracking the company controls, each funded modestly. A week is long enough to learn whether a channel is open, whether it converts at all, and roughly what an outcome costs at small scale.

A written answer. Which channel read, which did not, what each cost, what was ruled out and why, and what the next step should be, priced. The ruled-out list is the most durable page, because it stops the same arguments recurring every quarter.

BandWhat it meansExample of what the map recordsWhat the diagnostic does with it
OpenThe platform carries the category under its standard rulesNormal ad review, no certificationCandidate for a test this week
ConditionalAllowed with certification, licensing or country limitsGoogle certification plus a local licence for crypto exchange ads in a named countryRecords the conditions and lead time; tests only if already met
ClosedThe platform does not carry the category, or not in this marketNo permitted route for the product in that countryRuled out in writing, with the reason

The band map is not a one-off. Platform rules move. Google's cryptocurrency policy, for example, permitted exchange and software wallet ads in Argentina from September 2025 for advertisers on the national securities regulator's registry and certified by Google, and in Indonesia from February 2026 for advertisers licensed by the Financial Services Authority. A map dated six months ago can be wrong in both directions, which is why it is written down with a date. Our explainer on what a restricted category is covers how the conditional band works.

What one week cannot tell you

Long-run customer value. Seasonal effects. How a channel behaves at ten times the volume. Whether a restricted-band approval will arrive. Whether a partner program will produce in month six what it produced in week one.

A diagnostic that claims to answer those questions is overselling. What it can do is close the question of where the next dollar goes, which is more than most companies know when they spend it.

The platforms say the same about their own tests. Google's guidance for Google Ads experiments recommends running them for at least four to six weeks, longer where there is a long conversion delay, and waiting one to two conversion cycles before reading the result. A one-week test is therefore a read, not a controlled experiment. It answers "is this channel open, and does it convert at all at a cost worth pursuing", and it hands the controlled comparison to the next step. Our piece on campaign testing that reaches a decision covers sample sizes and holdouts for that next step, and A $10,000 test that closes a question beats a $10,000 bet that leaves it open makes the case for writing the question before the test starts.

A provider who offers all of that is selling you an answer. A provider who offers it free is selling you the engagement that follows.

How it differs from the alternatives

A free proposal is a sales document. Its cost is recovered in the engagement that follows, and its recommendations are shaped by what the provider wants to sell. It has no defined end and no obligation on the provider to be right. The cost is real: the European Association of Communications Agencies surveyed 412 agencies in 2025 and found the average new-business pitch cost about €43,800, with teams of five to eight people contributing more than 44 hours each.

An audit reviews what exists and lists what is wrong. Useful, but it does not test anything, so it produces opinions about channels rather than evidence from them.

A strategy engagement produces a plan, usually over several weeks, at consultancy rates, and leaves execution to someone else. Valuable for large, complex questions; oversized for "which channel should we try first."

Free proposalAuditStrategy engagementDistribution diagnostic
PaidNoYesYesYes
Defined endNoUsuallyYes, after several weeksYes, fixed
Tests channelsNoNoRarelyYes, two or three small tests
OutputPitch for the next engagementList of problemsA planA written answer, ruled-out list and priced next step
Obligation on the provider to be rightNoneLimitedOn the analysisOn the answer it writes down

A diagnostic is smaller than a strategy engagement, more evidence-based than an audit, and, because it is paid and scoped, more honest than a free proposal.

What to insist on

A fixed price and a fixed end date. A written question the work will answer. Tracking in your own name. Small real tests rather than desk research alone. A written output you can act on without hiring the provider. And the next step priced in the same document, so you know what continuing would cost before you decide whether to.

Tracking in your own name matters more than it sounds. If the test runs in the provider's ad account or analytics property, the evidence leaves when they do. Our piece Build it to run without you lists the accounts to own, and demand generation economics covers how to turn a test's cost per outcome into a budget ceiling for the next quarter.

A provider who offers all of that is selling you an answer. A provider who offers it free is selling you the engagement that follows.

A distribution diagnostic is a paid, scoped week that maps which channels can carry your product, tests the likely ones cheaply, and tells you in writing where the next dollar should go. It cannot tell you the voyage's earnings. It can tell you whether there is water under the hull.

lowob takeaways

  • Ask for the four parts. A band map, a read of existing assets, two or three small parallel tests, and a written answer.
  • Date the band map. Platform rules change by country and by quarter.
  • Treat a week as a read. It closes "where does the next dollar go", not long-run value or scale.
  • Own the evidence. Fixed price and end date, tracking in your name, and the next step priced in the same document.

Common questions

What is a distribution diagnostic?

A short, paid, scoped assessment of which channels can carry a product to its buyer, what each costs, and where the next serious money should go, with a fixed duration, fixed price, written output and no obligation to continue.

How is a distribution diagnostic different from a marketing audit?

An audit reviews what exists and lists what is wrong but tests nothing, so it gives opinions about channels. A diagnostic runs small real tests and gives evidence.

How long should a marketing channel test run?

Long enough to answer its question. A week can show whether a channel is open and converts at all. For a controlled comparison, Google recommends at least four to six weeks, and longer with a long conversion delay.

Should I accept a free strategy proposal from an agency?

A free proposal is a sales document shaped by what the provider wants to sell, with no defined end and no obligation to be right. A provider who offers it free is selling the engagement that follows.
